description: PalmSAR Innovators is a multidisciplinary team exploring Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR), remote sensing, GIS, and GeoAI for sustainable oil palm agriculture. We aim to transform satellite data into innovative solutions for monitoring plantation conditions, vegetation dynamics, and environmental changes. We welcome collaborators with expertise in Earth observation, programming, artificial intelligence, and geospatial analysis to develop impactful, data-driven solutions.
summary:
PalmSAR Watch is an open workflow and interactive web application that uses NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) L-band observations to detect and date oil palm felling in Labuhanbatu, North Sumatra, Indonesia. The project processes NISAR Level-2 Geocoded Polarimetric Covariance (GCOV) data to produce a dual-polarisation Radar Vegetation Index (RVI) time series and a vegetation-change map. It identifies potential vegetation loss when both RVI and HV backscatter decrease beyond defined thresholds, helping distinguish canopy removal from changes that affect only one radar measurement.
Using ten NISAR acquisitions from 16 June to 14 October 2026 over a 1,109 km² study area, the initial analysis flagged 181.5 hectares of vegetation loss and 14.5 hectares of vegetation gain. Three compact felling events, each covering 3.2–5.0 hectares, were identified and dated from their radar time series. The project matters because frequent cloud cover often limits optical monitoring in Sumatra, while L-band radar can observe the land surface through clouds. The results are provisional and the accuracy assessment of 60 stratified reference points is still in progress.
details:
About PalmSAR Watch

PalmSAR Watch monitors vegetation change associated with oil palm felling and replanting. It converts a sequence of NISAR L-band GCOV observations into RVI and HV backscatter layers, compares the first and last dates in the observation stack, and classifies pixels as vegetation loss, vegetation gain, or stable. The web application allows users to inspect the maps and examine the complete radar time series for individual pixels.

System Architecture

  1. Searches the Alaska Satellite Facility (ASF) archive for NISAR GCOV granules intersecting the study area and selects a consistent dual-polarisation time series from track 40, ascending, frame 3.
  2. Streams and subsets the HHHH and HVHV measurements and relevant coordinate and projection datasets from the HDF5 products.
  3. Applies 5 × 5 multilooking in linear power to reduce speckle and create a 50 m grid from the native 10 m data. Pixels with HH backscatter below −20 dB and pixels marked invalid in the GCOV mask are excluded.
  4. Calculates the dual-polarisation Radar Vegetation Index using RVI = 4 × HV / (HH + HV), with HH and HV expressed as linear power.
  5. Compares the first acquisition (16 June 2026) and last acquisition (14 October 2026). Vegetation loss is classified where ΔRVI ≤ −0.25 and ΔHV ≤ −3 dB; vegetation gain where ΔRVI ≥ +0.25 and ΔHV ≥ +3 dB; all other pixels are classified as stable.
  6. Exports the change layers and displays them in a Streamlit application. Users can switch between RVI, ΔRVI, change classes and HV backscatter, select dates and opacity, and click pixels to view RVI and HV time series.

Project Goals

  1. Provides a cloud-independent way to monitor oil palm canopy change in a region where persistent cloud cover can limit optical satellite observations.
  2. Uses the 12-day NISAR repeat cycle to bracket the timing of detected felling events within a period of a few weeks.
  3. Combines RVI and HV backscatter so that a change must appear in both measurements, reducing false alarms compared with relying on one indicator alone.
  4. Makes radar results easier to inspect through an interactive map and pixel-level time-series plots, without requiring users to operate specialist SAR software.
  5. Uses free and open NISAR data and an open-source Python workflow that can be rerun for other areas with suitable NISAR dual-polarisation coverage.

Key Features & Benefits

The project aims to provide a reproducible method for identifying where and approximately when oil palm stands are felled. Its longer-term goal is to support plantation monitoring, smallholder replanting programmes, land-use reporting and research. Planned improvements include completing the 60-point accuracy assessment, tuning the thresholds, adding a persistence rule and rainfall information to reduce moisture-related false alarms, reprocessing the full period with validated NISAR products, and extending the monitoring across North Sumatra.

Tools, coding languages, hardware and software

The workflow was developed in Python. The report identifies the following libraries and services: asf_search for searching the ASF archive; earthaccess for authenticated NASA Earthdata access and remote data streaming; h5py for reading HDF5 data; xarray, rioxarray and rasterio for data handling and raster processing; Streamlit for the web application; Folium for interactive mapping; Plotly for time-series visualisation; and Copernicus Browser for viewing Sentinel-2 reference imagery. The report describes the workflow as running on a laptop but does not specify hardware models or configurations.
